protocol.legal_basis: Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA): 'This clinical practice guideline may only be used by pharmacists who have been approved by the Department of Health to participate in the Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot (EACPP) and are authorised to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA). This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.' (p.1)
protocol.supervision_model: Approved/authorised pharmacist prescribing under the EACPP (document's own terminology) with professional-judgement oversight: 'Pharmacists must exercise professional discretion and judgement consistent with their qualifications and legislative authority. This guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to undertake clinical assessments and to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual and the relevant standards of care, in consultation with the patient and/or their parent/caregiver.' (p.1). 'Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines.' (p.6)
protocol.scope_summary: EACPP clinical practice guideline for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis (AD), community pharmacy service 'restricted to patients aged 6 months or over' (p.1). Guideline overview flow (p.2): meet service and professional obligations (initial eligibility and suitability, informed consent including consent for communication with other health practitioners) -> patient history and assessment -> develop management plan (eczema action plan, non-pharmacological measures, pharmacotherapy) -> confirm management is appropriate -> communicate agreed management plan -> clinical review, with two side columns: 'Refer when' (12 criteria, p.3) and 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' (4 criteria, p.3). Severity is graded with SCORAD or EASI (p.5; mild < 25 SCORAD / < 7 EASI, moderate 25 to 50 SCORAD / 7.1 to 21 EASI, severe > 50 SCORAD / > 21.1 EASI). Mainstay of treatment for active AD is topical corticosteroids in combination with emollients, trigger avoidance and early treatment of infection (p.3); all product-level potency/dose/frequency/quantity detail is delegated to Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Atopic dermatitis), the Australian Medicines Handbook and the ASCIA Action Plan for Eczema. Follow-up consultation is 7 to 14 days after initiation of new therapy or treatment change (p.8), and total quantity prescribed (including repeats) must not exceed 12 months supply (p.8).

inclusion.text: Service restricted to patients aged 6 months or over.
Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service (first step of the guideline overview flow).
Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant).
Patient history and assessment completed: 'Obtain sufficient information from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.'

Atopic dermatitis diagnosed clinically on patient history and physical findings: 'Both pruritus and a rash must be present for a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis (AD)'; 'For a diagnosis of AD to be made, both signs of itching and a rash must be present'; 'AD is usually diagnosed clinically, based on patient history and physical findings.'

Severity of AD assessed as within the scope of this guideline (mild to moderate): 'mild AD is indicated by a score of < 25 (SCORAD) or < 7 (EASI)'; 'moderate AD is indicated by a score 25 to 50 (SCORAD) or 7.1 to 21 (EASI)'. Severe AD ('severe AD is indicated by a score > 50 (SCORAD) or > 21.1 (EASI)') requires referral.
The patient does not meet any of the 12 'Refer when' criteria listed on page 3 (confirm before managing within the service).

exclusion.text: the patient is aged below 6 months (does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care)
raised purple rash that doesn't blanch
blistering of skin and mucous membranes (including mouth and eyes)
systemic signs or symptoms, including fever, lethargy, nausea, vomiting, headache

severe symptoms (SCORAD score > 51 or EASI score > 21.1) [the Severity section on page 5 instead prints 'severe AD is indicated by a score > 50 (SCORAD) or > 21.1 (EASI)' - both readings recorded, not reconciled]
child with a history of immediate or delayed-type hypersensitivity to food, poor feeding or sleep, concerns about failure to thrive
presentations with eczema herpeticum or cellulitis

exclusion_exceptions.text: Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.
(does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care) [printed against EXC-1, 'the patient is aged below 6 months']

If impetigo is present, it can be treated by the pharmacist as per the WA Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot Clinical Practice Guideline for Impetigo; 'suspected impetigo can be assessed and treated as per the WA Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot Clinical Practice Guideline for Impetigo or referred to an appropriate healthcare provider' [alternative management path within the secondary bacterial infection complication, which otherwise requires referral for cellulitis]

steps.description: Meet service and professional obligations - 'Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service'. Scope statement: 'Service restricted to patients aged 6 months or over.' Screen the patient against the 'Refer when' list (12 criteria, page 3) before accepting them into the service: 'Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider (including emergency services if required) in the following situations...'. 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

gates.criterion: Patient is suitable for management within the scope of the service and meets none of the 12 'Refer when' criteria (page 3)

steps.description: Obtain 'Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)'.

gates.criterion: Informed consent obtained, including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant

steps.description: Patient history and assessment. 'Obtain sufficient information from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.' The patient history should consider: age; weight; pregnancy and lactation status (if applicable); onset, duration, nature, location, severity and extent of patches and plaques, including recent or previous relapses or flare ups; response to any previous treatment/s; impacts on quality of life and psychosocial wellbeing including sleep and learning; dietary history and changes in diet; underlying and associated medical conditions including asthma, allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, allergic contact dermatitis, food allergy, and depression; exposure to potential triggers or irritants; other factors including family history, environmental factors (e.g. exposure to smoking and airborne pollution) and infectious factors; current and recently ceased treatments (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse drug reactions. 'Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies, and current medical conditions.' A comprehensive assessment template to assist with patient history is provided at Appendix 1.

gates.criterion: Sufficient information obtained to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines

steps.description: Examination - clinical features and severity (see Appendix 1 for template). 'AD is characterised by dry, scaly erythematous patches with the primary hallmark being itch.' While AD can affect any area of skin, patches typically occur on: the face; inside of the elbow/arm and back of the knee (cubital and popliteal fossae); wrists and ankles. 'For a diagnosis of AD to be made, both signs of itching and a rash must be present.' 'The skin signs of AD may vary depending on age and ethnicity.' 'People with AD are at higher risk of allergic contact reactions (e.g. nickel is a common contact allergen) and are prone to other viral skin infections (e.g. common warts and molluscum contagiosum).' 'AD is usually diagnosed clinically, based on patient history and physical findings.' For patients without an existing diagnosis of AD, other conditions with similar clinical features, symptoms and presentations that may be considered are outlined in Dermnet NZ: Guidelines for the diagnosis and assessment of eczema.

gates.criterion: Both signs of itching and a rash are present (required for a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis)
Diagnosis is clear (alternative similar conditions considered for patients without an existing diagnosis of AD)

steps.description: Assess severity with a scoring index. 'For the purposes of the service, the SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) index or the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) can be used to assess the severity of the AD to determine whether the patient requires referral, to inform the treatment plan and to monitor treatment effectiveness: mild AD is indicated by a score of < 25 (SCORAD) or < 7 (EASI); moderate AD is indicated by a score 25 to 50 (SCORAD) or 7.1 to 21 (EASI); severe AD is indicated by a score > 50 (SCORAD) or > 21.1 (EASI).' 'Conventional scoring systems may underestimate AD severity and erythema in people with darker skin tones. Consider the skin tone when assessing erythema and where there is uncertainty, severity can be assessed by using the EASI and upgrading the score by one grade or more for heavily pigmented skin (e.g. from mild to moderate).' Note: the 'Refer when' list on page 3 instead prints the severe threshold as 'SCORAD score > 51 or EASI score > 21.1'; both readings are recorded and are not reconciled (see open question).

gates.criterion: Severity assessed as mild or moderate (SCORAD < 25 or 25 to 50; EASI < 7 or 7.1 to 21), i.e. not severe (SCORAD > 50 per page 5 / > 51 per page 3; EASI > 21.1)

steps.description: Develop management plan. 'Pharmacist management of mild to moderate AD involves: development of an Eczema Action Plan - based on the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (ASCIA) Action Plan for Eczema template; non-pharmacological measures - advice regarding skin care and minimising aggravating factors as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Atopic dermatitis) and the Australian Medicines Handbook: Eczema; pharmacotherapy - a topical treatment for the management of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Atopic dermatitis).' 'The mainstay of treatment for active AD is topical corticosteroids (TCS) in combination with emollients, identification and avoidance of triggers, and the early treatment of infection.' 'Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines.' NB1: 'Very potent TCS (class IV), and potent TCS (class III containing betamethasone dipropionate 0.05 per cent, betamethasone valerate 0.1 per cent, methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 per cent, or mometasone furoate 0.1 per cent) should not be used for children aged 12 months or younger.' 'Selecting the correct potency and formulation of TCS is important to avoid both undertreatment and fears around TCS use.' 'Therapeutic regimens for AD can be expensive and complicated, making long-term compliance difficult and leading to poor outcomes. Choice of treatment should consider the impact of factors such as age, socioeconomic status, cost and literacy on the patient's ability to adhere to prescribed therapies.' Pharmacist consultation sources: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Considerations in the use of topical corticosteroids); Australian Medicines Handbook: Corticosteroids (skin); Australasian College of Dermatologists consensus statements (management of atopic dermatitis in adults; topical corticosteroids in paediatric eczema); Australian Journal of General Practice: Selection of an effective topical corticosteroid.

gates.criterion: Management plan includes an Eczema Action Plan (ASCIA template), non-pharmacological measures (skin care and minimising aggravating factors) and a topical treatment in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Atopic dermatitis)

TCS potency appropriate for age: very potent TCS (class IV) and potent TCS (class III containing betamethasone dipropionate 0.05 per cent, betamethasone valerate 0.1 per cent, methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 per cent, or mometasone furoate 0.1 per cent) are not used for children aged 12 months or younger

steps.description: Confirm management is appropriate - 'Consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other resources to confirm that management is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation.'

gates.criterion: No contraindications, precautions or drug interactions identified for the proposed treatment
Patient is not planning a pregnancy, is not, and could not be pregnant (otherwise treat and concurrently refer)

steps.description: Communicate agreed management plan. 'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use (e.g. application instructions for emollients, topical treatments, and wet dressing use); non-pharmacological measures; how to manage adverse effects; when to seek further care and/or treatment, including recognising secondary infection; when to return for follow-up.' 'It is the pharmacist's responsibility to ensure the suitability and accuracy of any resources and information provided to patients (and/or parents/caregivers if applicable), and to ensure compliance with all copyright conditions.' 'The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent.' 'When recommending TCS for AD, pharmacists should reassure patients (and/or parents/caregivers) who have concerns about the safety of TCS that they are safe when used appropriately.' 'Patients (and/or parents/caregivers) should be counselled on the role of emollients in both the management of AD, and the ongoing maintenance of remission after the flare is clear and TCS treatment is ceased. Advice regarding skin care and minimising aggravating factors should be reiterated.' 'Common adverse effects of TCS, such as transient burning, stinging or pain on application, can generally be reversed by stopping the medicine.'

gates.criterion: Agreed management plan communicated (product use, non-pharmacological measures, adverse effect management, when to seek further care, when to return for follow-up) and shared with the multidisciplinary healthcare team with consent

steps.description: Clinical review. 'Clinical review with the pharmacist (or the patient's chosen healthcare provider) should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines.' 'Patients should return for a follow up consultation 7 to 14 days after initiation of a new therapy and/or changes to the treatment plan. Clinical review should consider: response to treatment (using the SCORAD index or EASI); if changes are required to the treatment plan. Decisions to continue, modify or stop treatment should be reflected in the patient's eczema action plan. If a good response has been achieved, the medication can be stopped, and the patient can continue using regular emollients to maintain remission. If there has been an inadequate response, the pharmacist should check the patient's compliance with the medication and skin care measures, ensuring enough medication is applied. For patients continuing therapy, follow-up should be individualised to the patient's clinical presentation, response to treatment, and therapeutic goals. Pharmacists should prescribe a quantity of medicine (including repeats) that aligns with the expected duration of therapy, ensuring sufficient supply until the patient's next review. The total quantity prescribed should not exceed 12 months supply (including repeats).'

gates.criterion: Response to treatment assessed at the 7 to 14 day follow up consultation (SCORAD or EASI)

diagnosis_pathways.name: Refer when / treat and concurrently refer triage (page 3), with general advice on when to seek further care (page 7)

steps.description: Screen against the 'Refer when' criteria: 'Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider (including emergency services if required) in the following situations: the patient is aged below 6 months (does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care); unclear diagnosis; widespread rash with painful skin; raised purple rash that doesn't blanch; > 90 per cent skin involvement (urgent referral); blistering of skin and mucous membranes (including mouth and eyes); systemic signs or symptoms, including fever, lethargy, nausea, vomiting, headache; chronic sores or ulcers; severe symptoms (SCORAD score > 51 or EASI score > 21.1); child with a history of immediate or delayed-type hypersensitivity to food, poor feeding or sleep, concerns about failure to thrive; presentations with eczema herpeticum or cellulitis; inadequate response to optimal treatment.'

gates.criterion: None of the 12 'Refer when' criteria is present

steps.description: Refer to an appropriate healthcare provider (including emergency services if required). '> 90 per cent skin involvement' requires urgent referral. 'If cellulitis is present the patient should be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.' 'suspected cellulitis must be referred to an appropriate health care provider.' 'refer to an appropriate healthcare provider if eczema herpeticum is suspected.' Secondary bacterial infection (e.g. secondary impetigo or cellulitis) is a common complication of AD; treatment of concurrent infection is important for successful management of active AD.

gates.criterion: Referral destination and urgency arranged; urgent referral where skin involvement is > 90 per cent

steps.description: 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer - Provide initial treatment and concurrently refer to an appropriate healthcare provider in the following situations: > 30 per cent skin involvement; the patient is planning a pregnancy, is, or could be pregnant; the patient is immunocompromised or has diabetes; quality of life is significantly affected.'

gates.criterion: Where any 'treat and concurrently refer' criterion is present: initial treatment provided (if clinically appropriate) AND concurrent referral to an appropriate healthcare provider made

provenance.section_heading: Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer

steps.description: General advice - 'At the time of initial consultation, patients (and/or parents/caregivers if applicable) should be advised to see an appropriate healthcare provider if: signs or symptoms worsen; new signs or symptoms occur (including systemic signs or symptoms); there is inadequate improvement of symptoms within 1 to 2 weeks; symptoms recur within 2 to 4 weeks of initial resolution; stable, long-term control of the condition is not achieved; ongoing impairment is present e.g. pruritus, pain, loss of sleep, learning difficulties; quality of life is significantly affected.'

gates.criterion: All seven 'see an appropriate healthcare provider if' triggers have been advised at the initial consultation

treatments.form: topical preparation (specific formulation not printed; 'Selecting the correct potency and formulation of TCS is important')
treatments.strength: class IV (very potent); class III (potent) containing betamethasone dipropionate 0.05 per cent, betamethasone valerate 0.1 per cent, methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 per cent, or mometasone furoate 0.1 per cent
treatments.max_quantity: Total quantity prescribed (including repeats) should not exceed 12 months supply (p.8).
treatments.quantity_to_supply: quantity aligned with the expected duration of therapy, ensuring sufficient supply until the patient's next review; total quantity prescribed (including repeats) must not exceed 12 months supply
treatments.notes: 'The mainstay of treatment for active AD is topical corticosteroids (TCS) in combination with emollients, identification and avoidance of triggers, and the early treatment of infection' (p.3). Pharmacotherapy for mild to moderate AD is 'a topical treatment ... in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Atopic dermatitis)' (p.6) - no dose, frequency, application site, quantity or product-level strength is printed in this document; those must be taken from the specified sections of the current online Therapeutic Guidelines. NB1 (verbatim, p.6): 'Very potent TCS (class IV), and potent TCS (class III containing betamethasone dipropionate 0.05 per cent, betamethasone valerate 0.1 per cent, methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 per cent, or mometasone furoate 0.1 per cent) should not be used for children aged 12 months or younger.' 'Selecting the correct potency and formulation of TCS is important to avoid both undertreatment and fears around TCS use.' 'Therapeutic regimens for AD can be expensive and complicated, making long-term compliance difficult and leading to poor outcomes. Choice of treatment should consider the impact of factors such as age, socioeconomic status, cost and literacy on the patient's ability to adhere to prescribed therapies.' 'NB2: Underuse of TCS is a common cause of previous treatment failure' (p.10). Common adverse effects of TCS, such as transient burning, stinging or pain on application, can generally be reversed by stopping the medicine; 'Refer to an appropriate healthcare provider when adverse effects cannot be managed in the pharmacy setting' (p.7). 'When recommending TCS for AD, pharmacists should reassure patients (and/or parents/caregivers) who have concerns about the safety of TCS that they are safe when used appropriately' (p.7). Pregnancy/lactation: confirm management is appropriate including for pregnancy and lactation (p.6); a patient planning a pregnancy, who is, or could be pregnant requires treat-and-concurrently-refer (p.3).

treatments.frequency: regular ('continue using regular emollients to maintain remission')
treatments.duration: ongoing - 'the role of emollients in both the management of AD, and the ongoing maintenance of remission after the flare is clear and TCS treatment is ceased'
treatments.notes: Used in combination with TCS as part of the mainstay of treatment for active AD (p.3). 'Patients (and/or parents/caregivers) should be counselled on the role of emollients in both the management of AD, and the ongoing maintenance of remission after the flare is clear and TCS treatment is ceased. Advice regarding skin care and minimising aggravating factors should be reiterated' (p.7). 'If a good response has been achieved, the medication can be stopped, and the patient can continue using regular emollients to maintain remission' (p.8). Assessment template records 'emollient/moisturiser use, application frequency, and quantity applied' (p.10); 'emollients containing sodium lauryl sulphate' are listed as an identification-of-triggers irritant (p.10). No product, strength, quantity or application frequency is printed; 'how to use the soak and smear technique' is referred to Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (p.8).

Referenced only as counselling content: 'individual product and medicine use (e.g. application instructions for emollients, topical treatments, and wet dressing use)' (p.7), and as a patient resource: 'Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Atopic dermatitis - How to apply a wet dressing)' and '(Atopic dermatitis - How to use the soak and smear technique)' (p.8). No solution, product, frequency, duration or quantity is printed in this document - the technique is external to the protocol.

routine: Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider (including emergency services if required) in the following situations (routine unless stated otherwise): the patient is aged below 6 months (does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care); unclear diagnosis; widespread rash with painful skin; raised purple rash that doesn't blanch; blistering of skin and mucous membranes (including mouth and eyes); systemic signs or symptoms, including fever, lethargy, nausea, vomiting, headache; chronic sores or ulcers; severe symptoms (SCORAD score > 51 or EASI score > 21.1); child with a history of immediate or delayed-type hypersensitivity to food, poor feeding or sleep, concerns about failure to thrive; presentations with eczema herpeticum or cellulitis; inadequate response to optimal treatment.

Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer - provide initial treatment and concurrently refer to an appropriate healthcare provider: > 30 per cent skin involvement; the patient is planning a pregnancy, is, or could be pregnant; the patient is immunocompromised or has diabetes; quality of life is significantly affected.
If cellulitis is present the patient should be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.
suspected impetigo can be assessed and treated as per the WA Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot Clinical Practice Guideline for Impetigo or referred to an appropriate healthcare provider
refer to an appropriate healthcare provider if eczema herpeticum is suspected.
Refer to an appropriate healthcare provider when adverse effects cannot be managed in the pharmacy setting.
The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent.

At the time of initial consultation, patients (and/or parents/caregivers if applicable) should be advised to see an appropriate healthcare provider if: signs or symptoms worsen; new signs or symptoms occur (including systemic signs or symptoms); there is inadequate improvement of symptoms within 1 to 2 weeks; symptoms recur within 2 to 4 weeks of initial resolution; stable, long-term control of the condition is not achieved; ongoing impairment is present e.g. pruritus, pain, loss of sleep, learning difficulties; quality of life is significantly affected.
emergency: Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider (including emergency services if required) in the following situations: [all 12 'Refer when' criteria, page 3 - emergency services only 'if required', no further urgency grading printed for individual criteria]

review_followup.what: Follow up consultation with the pharmacist (or the patient's chosen healthcare provider); clinical review should consider response to treatment (using the SCORAD index or EASI) and whether changes are required to the treatment plan.

review_followup.when: at the follow up consultation, where changes are required
review_followup.what: Decisions to continue, modify or stop treatment should be reflected in the patient's eczema action plan.

review_followup.when: once a good response has been achieved
review_followup.what: The medication can be stopped, and the patient can continue using regular emollients to maintain remission.

review_followup.when: if there has been an inadequate response
review_followup.what: Check the patient's compliance with the medication and skin care measures, ensuring enough medication is applied.

Follow-up should be individualised to the patient's clinical presentation, response to treatment, and therapeutic goals; clinical review with the pharmacist (or the patient's chosen healthcare provider) should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines.

review_followup.when: at any time after initial consultation, if any of the seven general advice triggers occur (worsening; new signs or symptoms; inadequate improvement within 1 to 2 weeks; recurrence within 2 to 4 weeks; no stable long-term control; ongoing impairment; quality of life significantly affected)

conditions: The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent (p.7).

Consent must be obtained for communication with other health practitioners if relevant: 'Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)' (p.2).
Communication with other health practitioners is an explicit step of the guideline overview flow (p.2).

open_questions.topic: SCORAD severe threshold contradicts itself between page 3 and page 5 - both readings recorded
open_questions.observed: 'Refer when' (p.3) prints 'severe symptoms (SCORAD score > 51 or EASI score > 21.1)'; the Severity section (p.5) prints 'severe AD is indicated by a score > 50 (SCORAD) or > 21.1 (EASI)'. The EASI thresholds agree (> 21.1); the SCORAD threshold does not (> 51 vs > 50).
open_questions.why_unclear: The two printed thresholds differ by one point, so a SCORAD of exactly 50.5 (or a score of 51 under the page 5 rule) is referral-or-not depending on which page is encoded. Spec forbids silent reconciliation: EXC-9/RF-9 carry the page 3 reading with confidence 'unclear', RF-15 carries the page 5 reading, and hugh_to_confirm asks which threshold to encode.

open_questions.topic: Combinatorics of the eligibility decision list are not printed
open_questions.observed: The guideline prints an eligibility flow (p.2) with downward arrows between boxes and the referral list as 'in the following situations:' (p.3); no explicit AND/OR statement appears anywhere.
open_questions.why_unclear: Inclusion criteria were given all_of (sequential flow boxes, each of which must be met, plus the age restriction and the diagnosis/severity requirements); exclusion criteria were given any_of because 'in the following situations' reads as any one triggering referral. Confidence on the inclusion members is therefore 'medium' rather than 'high'.

open_questions.topic: Two-column layout on page 2 and garbled resource list on page 9
open_questions.observed: Page 2 prints the flow ('Meet service and professional obligations' ... 'Clinical review') in the left column and 'Refer when' / 'Treat and concurrently refer' in the right column; the flat text extraction interleaves the columns line by line. Page 9 ('Pharmacist resources') extracts with doubled characters ('PPhhaarrmmaacciisstt rreessoouurrcceess') and interleaved bulleted lists from adjacent columns.
open_questions.why_unclear: The page 2 flow order was reconstructed from the printed arrows and cross-checked against the full lists on page 3 (the right column of page 2 repeats page 3 verbatim). The page 9 resource titles could not be reliably separated, so no structured field draws on page 9; the numbered references (pages 11-12) are unaffected.

open_questions.topic: No product-level dosing, potency choice or quantity printed for any treatment
open_questions.observed: 'Pharmacotherapy: a topical treatment for the management of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Atopic dermatitis)'; emollients and wet dressings are mentioned with no product, strength, dose, frequency or quantity; 'Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines.'
open_questions.why_unclear: TX-1, TX-2 and TX-3 therefore have blank dose/frequency/max_dose fields; only the named TCS classes and molecules on page 6 carry printed strengths. Nothing can be transcribed without inventing it.

open_questions.topic: TCS potency selection rule by severity, site and age is external
open_questions.observed: 'Selecting the correct potency and formulation of TCS is important to avoid both undertreatment and fears around TCS use', but the document does not state which class to use for mild vs moderate disease, body site, or age (beyond the class III/IV prohibition in children aged 12 months or younger).
open_questions.why_unclear: The potency-selection logic cannot be encoded from this document; it must come from Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Considerations in the use of topical corticosteroids) and the two Australasian College of Dermatologists consensus statements listed as consultation sources.

open_questions.topic: Age bound printed in months, expressed in years in age_bounds
open_questions.observed: 'Service restricted to patients aged 6 months or over' (p.1) and 'the patient is aged below 6 months' (p.3). No upper age bound is printed.
open_questions.why_unclear: age_bounds.min_years is expressed as 0.5 to represent the printed '6 months'; max_years is null because no numeric upper bound exists in the document.

open_questions.topic: Gate on_fail not stated for several pathway gates
open_questions.observed: The document does not state what happens when consent cannot be obtained (PW-1-S2), when history is insufficient (PW-1-S3), when the management plan/potency check fails (PW-1-S6), when the plan cannot be communicated (PW-1-S8), when the 7-14 day review is missed (PW-1-S9), when referral destination/urgency cannot be arranged (PW-2-S2), or when the general advice triggers are not advised (PW-2-S4).
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires on_fail 'unclear' plus an open question where the document is silent; these are recorded as 'unclear' rather than inferred. Note that pregnancy/lactation and the failed severity/diagnosis gates do have printed on_fail (concurrent referral / referral), so those are encoded as REFER.

open_questions.topic: Urgency language appears only once in the document
open_questions.observed: Only '> 90 per cent skin involvement' carries an explicit '(urgent referral)' tag (p.3); the referral preamble says '(including emergency services if required)' without naming any criterion; eczema herpeticum 'may be fatal' (p.5); the 'Treat and concurrently refer' and 'General advice' lists carry no urgency wording at all.
open_questions.why_unclear: Severity assignments follow the document's own language only: high for the explicit urgent item and the fatal-risk herpeticum statement, medium for plain referrals, low for treat-and-refer and general advice, with no escalation to 'critical' anywhere because the document prints no ambulance/000 trigger.

open_questions.topic: No measurement method for skin involvement percentages
open_questions.observed: The document uses '> 30 per cent skin involvement' and '> 90 per cent skin involvement' thresholds but prints no body surface area assessment method; 'Fingertip unit' appears only as a title in the page 9 resource list.
open_questions.why_unclear: The engine cannot compute skin involvement from printed instructions; the structured checks RF-5 and RF-16 depend on a measurement method that must be chosen locally.

open_questions.topic: 'Inadequate response to optimal treatment' is undefined
open_questions.observed: 'inadequate response to optimal treatment.' is a refer-when criterion (p.3) with no definition of 'optimal treatment', no minimum trial duration and no named severity score.
open_questions.why_unclear: RF-12/EXC-12 transcribe the phrase verbatim with structured null; a rules engine cannot evaluate it without a local definition (7-14 day review interval is the only nearby timing anchor, p.8).

open_questions.topic: No systemic pharmacotherapy is recommended anywhere in this guideline
open_questions.observed: 'Antihistamine and antibiotic use' appear only as items to assess in the patient history (Appendix 1, p.10); secondary infection treatment is deferred to the separate Impetigo guideline (p.3, p.5); no oral corticosteroid, antibiotic, antihistamine or immunomodulator is prescribed or described.
open_questions.why_unclear: No treatment rows were created for antihistamines or antibiotics because the document makes no recommendation about them; if the prescribing support module is expected to cover systemic therapy for AD, that content is outside this instrument.

open_questions.topic: Referral block provenance spans pages 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7
open_questions.observed: Referral destinations and criteria appear on page 1 (usual pharmacy care statement), page 2 (flow columns), page 3 (the full lists), page 5 (complications) and page 7 (general advice and adverse effects).
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec allows one shared provenance for the referral block using the first page of the full list; page 3 recorded, with the range noted here.

open_questions.topic: No version number or effective date printed
open_questions.observed: Page 13 footer codes read "62'GUA" and "80510-DEC"; the document shows © Department of Health 2026, 'Produced by Clinical Excellence Division', and references up to 2025 sources, but no protocol version/date.
open_questions.why_unclear: instrument_version and effective_date could not be filled from a printed identifier.

open_questions.topic: Consent documentation content is not specified
open_questions.observed: 'Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)' (p.2) is required, but no consent form, wording or record location is printed in this document.
open_questions.why_unclear: PW-1-S2 gate on_fail is recorded as 'unclear' and the consent content must come from Pilot materials outside this protocol.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Encode the SCORAD severe-referral threshold: page 3 says '> 51', page 5 says '> 50' - choose which one the rules engine enforces (both readings are recorded; EXC-9/RF-9 are marked 'unclear').
hugh_to_confirm.reason: A contradictory threshold cannot be evaluated automatically; the choice determines whether SCORAD 51 (or 50-51) patients are referred or treated in the pharmacy.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Encode topical corticosteroid potency selection (which class for mild vs moderate, body site, age, and face/flexures) from the current online Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology (Considerations in the use of topical corticosteroids) - none of it is printed in this protocol.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: TX-1 is first-line therapy but the document supplies only the class III/IV examples and the paediatric prohibition; a prescribing support module cannot select a product from this instrument alone.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Encode the paediatric TCS potency restriction as a hard prescribing check: 'Very potent TCS (class IV), and potent TCS (class III containing betamethasone dipropionate 0.05 per cent, betamethasone valerate 0.1 per cent, methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 per cent, or mometasone furoate 0.1 per cent) should not be used for children aged 12 months or younger.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: This is the only numeric medicine-safety rule printed in the document and it must block supply, not merely advise; the document states no on_fail action for breaching it.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the measurement method for the '> 30 per cent' and '> 90 per cent skin involvement' thresholds (body surface area tool, rule of nines, or clinician estimate).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: RF-5 (urgent referral) and RF-16 (treat and concurrently refer) are percentage-based but no assessment method is printed anywhere in the document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Define locally what counts as 'optimal treatment' and the trial period for the refer-when criterion 'inadequate response to optimal treatment'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The criterion is unbounded as printed; without a definition the rules engine cannot decide when a non-responding patient must be referred (the nearest anchor is the 7 to 14 day follow-up, p.8).

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local supply policy for the printed cap: 'The total quantity prescribed should not exceed 12 months supply (including repeats)' and 'Pharmacists should prescribe a quantity of medicine (including repeats) that aligns with the expected duration of therapy, ensuring sufficient supply until the patient's next review'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Quantity-to-supply depends on the local review schedule; the 12-month ceiling is the only printed cap and must be enforced at dispensing.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm pharmacist EACPP approval and authorisation status per the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA): 'This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Prescribing under the protocol is conditional on individual Department of Health approval, which is not verifiable from the document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Obtain the consent documentation requirements for participation, including consent for communication with other health practitioners (no consent wording or form is printed in this document).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Consent is a gating step (PW-1-S2) and also the condition attached to sharing the management plan (notifiable.conditions), but its required content and record format are external.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm whether antihistamines and/or antibiotics are within pharmacist prescribing scope for this service: the document lists 'antihistamine and antibiotic use' only as history to assess, defers infection treatment to the separate Impetigo guideline, and prescribes no systemic therapy.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: If the module is expected to act on pruritus or secondary infection, the medicines, doses and authority must come from another instrument - nothing is prescribable from this document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the EASI grading-uplift rule for pigmented skin as an encoded step: 'where there is uncertainty, severity can be assessed by using the EASI and upgrading the score by one grade or more for heavily pigmented skin (e.g. from mild to moderate)'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The rule is a judgement uplift that changes whether a patient is in scope (mild/moderate) or must be referred (severe); the document gives no decision threshold for 'uncertainty' or 'heavily pigmented'.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the clinical review schedule source: 'Clinical review with the pharmacist (or the patient's chosen healthcare provider) should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines' - the specific intervals beyond the printed 7 to 14 day follow-up are external.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: FU-1 to FU-5 depend on external review intervals; only the 7 to 14 day window is printed, so the ongoing review cadence cannot be scheduled from this instrument.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local process for handling treat-and-concurrently-refer patients (> 30 per cent skin involvement, pregnancy/planning pregnancy, immunocompromised or diabetes, significantly affected quality of life): supply first or refer first, and what treatment is 'clinically appropriate' to supply.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The document requires initial treatment AND concurrent referral but does not sequence them or define the medicines that may be supplied in that visit.
